title: Neonatal Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: 89 Neonatal Necrotizing Enterocolitis
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), first described over 60 years ago, is the most significant contributor to preterm infant gastrointestinal morbidity and mortality. Its pathogenesis remains poorly understood despite considerable research efforts, and prevention and treatment remain significant challenges. Improved survival of large numbers of extremely vulnerable preterm infants likely plays a role, but there are other reasons, as well. NEC is complicated to define. Instead of being a discrete disease entity, it is better described as a diagnostic category encompassing several more discrete forms of intestinal injury and dysfunctions that have yet to be clearly delineated. This chapter discusses historical perspectives, our current understanding of pathophysiology, prevention, treatment, and future directions to differentiate the more discrete patterns of intestinal dysfunction and injury under the broad diagnosis of NEC. Because the authors still do not have a precise term to describe these more discrete injuries and dysfunctions, not all of which involve intestinal necrosis, we will continue to refer to a diagnosis considered to engender an inflammatory cascade in its pathogenesis as classic NEC. The rationale for doing this is based on clinical and laboratory findings that this form of intestinal injury is often accompanied by clinical deterioration and clear signs of intestinal inflammation, including abdominal distension, periumbilical erythema, bloody stools, the elevation of nonspecific inflammatory markers, and distinctive radiologic changes such as pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: As discussed, NEC is an antiquated term, and the forms of intestinal injury and dysfunction that are currently diagnosed require a thorough re-examination. These likely cluster under different pathophysiologic schemes. Accordingly, several entities that have been referred to as NEC (“imposters”) will be discussed, along with attempts to explain how they differ from the more classic inflammatory process. In addition to this delineation, we will also discuss some hypotheses related to the pathogenesis of the classic
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: inflammatory process, means of recognition, possible preventative strategies, treatment, and sequelae.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Several publications have recently discussed difficulties with defining NEC and the importance of having a more refined definition.1–4 This is highly problematic because a clear definition of any given disease is required to provide a common foundation to study its epidemiology, pathogenesis, outcomes, and effectiveness of treatments. The lack of a clear definition for NEC has complicated efforts to study this disease. The pathophysiologies of conditions currently placed under the term NEC are very different. For example, the cascade of events leading to intestinal necrosis in a term infant with intestinal ischemia caused by a congenital heart lesion is very different when compared to a week-old extremely preterm infant who develops intestinal perforation and a peritoneal drain is placed without seeing the intestine; a 6-week-old preterm infant who develops abdominal distension, bloody stools, and eosinophilia; or a preterm neonate who has recurrent abdominal distension and emesis but never develops pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas on radiograph.
paragraphs.heading: Definition of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, all of these have been referred to as NEC. Grouping multiple conditions under one diagnostic umbrella of NEC affects the reliability of statistical data collected and stalls efforts to develop effective preventive and treatment strategies. This chapter recognizes the major shortcomings of what has been referred to as NEC but will still attempt to provide an overview of what this diagnosis entails.
paragraphs.heading: Definition of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: The incidence of NEC inversely correlates with gestational age at birth, with a higher incidence in babies born at lower gestational ages.5–7 In more than 90% of cases, NEC
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: develops in infants born at less than 37 weeks. In the United States, among infants whose gestational age ranged from 22 to 28 weeks, the incidence of NEC declined from 13% in 2008 to 9% in 2012.8 In another epidemiologic analysis, data were prospectively collected on very low birth weight (VLBW) infants (≤1500 g or <29 weeks) born from 2006 to 2017 and admitted to 820 US centers.9 Of 473,895 VLBW infants, 36,130 (7.6%) were diagnosed with NEC, of which 21,051 (58.3%) had medical NEC and 15,079 (41.7%) had surgical NEC. Medical NEC decreased from 5.3% to 3.0%. Surgical NEC decreased from 3.4% to 3.1%. Medical NEC mortality decreased from 20.7% to 16.8% (P = .003), and surgical NEC mortality decreased from 36.6% to 31.6%. Primary peritoneal drainage (PPD) versus initial laparotomy rose from 23.2% to 46.8% in the surgical cohort. Other risk factors associated with NEC, such as intrauterine growth restriction, placental abruption, the presence of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and prolonged antibiotic exposure, have been reported.10–12
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Early clinical signs of what we refer to as classic NEC are usually vague and nonspecific and may include slight changes in vital signs, new-onset or increased apneic episodes, feeding intolerance, and emesis. Deterioration becomes evident on physical examination as the disease progresses. The signs of disease advancement are also nonspecific: hypotonia, respiratory distress, and cardiovascular instability. The abdominal exam reveals distention, tenderness, discoloration of the abdominal wall, and lack of bowel sounds. Laboratory changes are notable for neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and metabolic acidosis. Blood may be noticed in gastric contents or stool. Classic NEC is historically discriminated from spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP) by the age of onset, with SIP occurring earlier in the admission course. Berrington and Embleton13 recently showed considerable overlap between NEC and SIP in those that present early (<14 days), and the two entities may not be accurately differentiated. In a cohort of 785 infants, NEC occurred before 14 days of life in 30% of the infants who had NEC.
paragraphs.heading: Presentation

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis is made using a combination of clinical, laboratory, and radiologic findings, with radiologic findings being more important for determining the severity of the disease process. NEC was systematically described, and staging criteria were proposed by Bell et al.14 in 1978, with modifications of staging made by Kliegman and Fanaroff15 in 1987. Modified Bell’s criteria are widely used for data collection and research; however, this classification has significant limitations. Stage I consists of a combination of highly nonspecific findings. It significantly distorts the incidence of NEC. Pneumatosis intestinalis, a hallmark of stage II disease, may
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: be difficult to find on radiographs. Additionally, heterogeneously appearing intestinal stool content may be misinterpreted as pneumatosis intestinalis (Fig. 89.1). A hallmark of stage III is perforated viscus with free intraperitoneal air, which could be due to SIP or NEC. A confirmed diagnosis remains unknown when a primary peritoneal drain is placed and no direct bowel visualization and histologic evaluation are performed. This classification also falls short when NEC progresses without exhibiting pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas. Even with free intraperitoneal air, if only a drain is placed without direct observation by the surgeon, the definitive diagnosis of NEC cannot be made. Several other scoring systems have been developed over the years that may be more useful in diagnosing NEC using machine learning techniques.2 The advent of machine learning analysis has recently led to the development of predictive tools to differentiate NEC with SIPs.16
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: It is important to note that available modes of diagnostics for NEC can only recognize changes in the late stages of the disease when the intestinal epithelial barrier has already been compromised and the signs of systemic response and deterioration are apparent. Complete blood count (CBC) components held promise as a biomarker for early NEC. Decreasing platelet counts, elevated immature to total neutrophil (I/T) ratio, and elevated or decreased neutrophil counts have been used as laboratory signs of NEC, with none specific to this disease.17,18 Multiple inflammatory and immunologic markers have been studied as potential predictive biomarkers of NEC. Among them are C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, an array of cytokines and
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: chemokines, platelet-activating factor (PAF), and interalpha inhibitory protein (IαIp), to name a few. So far, none of them has shown significant ability to do so.19 Markers of intestinal inflammation and injury such as fatty acid– binding protein (FABP), fecal calprotectin, and claudins are also being investigated.20,21 Their usefulness as early screening markers for NEC is questionable. Salivary epidermal growth factor (EGF) is increased in infants with NEC compared to those without NEC.22 The absence of a clear definition of NEC and limited understanding of its initial pathophysiologic changes impede the ability to develop reliable biomarkers of early disease. A list of biomarkers being studied to predict or diagnose NEC is provided in Table 89.1.20,23–26 A major caveat to the use of biomarkers lies in the difficulty with defining the different entities. Some biomarkers may be suitable for certain subcategories of intestinal injury and dysfunction but not for others.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: In recent years, high-throughput molecular techniques and systems biology approaches have been utilized to further study potential biomarkers for NEC. Proteomics, metabolomics, metagenomics, and transcriptomics are all relatively new advances in research technology promising to offer new biomarkers for NEC.23 Nonetheless, the absence of standard reference values for gestational and chronological age has been challenging, in addition to the lack of omic standard values accepted as a confirmation of NEC diagnosis.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Radiologic signs used to diagnose NEC include pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas (Fig. 89.2), free intraperitoneal air, distended and fixed bowel loops, and a gasless abdomen. However, studies have shown significant variability in the interpretation of abdominal radiographs of infants with suspected NEC.27,28
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Abdominal ultrasound is emerging as a modality as an adjunct in evaluating infants with suspected NEC.29 The purported advantages over x-ray are real-time imaging, the ability to assess the presence of peristalsis and detect even minimal ascites, accurate detection of intestinal wall thickness, and perfusion.30–33 A meta-analysis revealed sensitivities ranging 0.27 to 0.48 and specificities of more than 0.91 for NEC diagnosis.34 Abdominal ultrasound is promising as an adjunct to detecting early signs of NEC, which may lead to earlier and more aggressive treatment before the development of more advanced NEC. However, questions
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: remain about the sensitivity and specificity of ultrasound in NEC diagnosis compared to the gold standard of intestinal necrosis seen during surgery or autopsy. Furthermore, bowel ultrasound is operator dependent, comes with inter-reader variability, and has the potential lack of 24-hour availability; also, given its relatively innovative nature, many have not received formal training in using it to diagnose NEC. The above factors lead to uncertainty in diagnosing the early stages of intestinal injury, unnecessary exposure of significant numbers of extremely preterm infants to interruptions of enteral feedings and courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a prolonged need for central access. These interventions are associated with an increased incidence of late-onset sepsis, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and hospitalization.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Because of an incomplete understanding of the etiology of NEC, treatment modalities have focused chiefly on supportive measures such as stopping enteral feedings, decompressing the gastrointestinal tract, using broad-spectrum antibiotics, and correcting metabolic (acidosis) and hematologic (thrombocytopenia, anemia) derangements. Careful attention must be paid to maintaining normal cardiovascular and respiratory functions, which may involve the utilization of mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and fluid resuscitation.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Management

paragraphs.text: The choice of antibiotics usually depends on practice in each unit but generally consists of two broad-spectrum agents that cover intestinal microorganisms. Anaerobic coverage may be added, as well. A large propensity-matched study evaluated the effect of anaerobic coverage on the antimicrobial regimen.35 Overall, the infants in the anaerobic coverage group developed more strictures (odds ratio [OR] = 1.73; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11–2.72; P = .02). In infants with surgical NEC, death was significantly less common (OR = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.52–0.95; P = .02).35 Antimicrobial therapy may be tailored to a specific microorganism in cases of positive blood culture. The length of the antibiotic course usually ranges from 7 to 10 days. The decision to stop or prolong antimicrobial therapy is usually guided by clinical status and nonspecific laboratory markers of inflammation such as CRP. Few evidence-based data are available, however, to help clinicians determine the appropriate duration of antimicrobial therapy. It is also unclear how beneficial antibiotics are in NEC cases with negative blood cultures. Serial abdominal x-rays monitor the progression of radiologic findings and help determine the need for surgical intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Management

paragraphs.text: The main objectives of surgical intervention in NEC are to control enteric spillage and maximize the length of the viable intestine if resection is needed. Surgery is required in about
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Management

paragraphs.text: 30% to 40% of NEC cases, and pneumoperitoneum is the only absolute criterion for intervention.36,37 Clinical deterioration despite maximal medical management remains a relative indication for operative management. Tepas et al.38 proposed that the trajectory of metabolic derangement can predict the timing of surgical intervention. Blood culture, bandemia, acidosis, thrombocytopenia, hypotension, hyponatremia, and neutropenia were the seven criteria identified as possible predictors. Historically, exploratory laparotomy (ExLap) with resection of nonviable intestine has been a procedure of choice since the 1970s. However, PPD placement was initially utilized as a temporary measure in infants deemed too sick to tolerate ExLap. PPD placement became more accepted as definitive therapy after reports supporting this approach were published in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) aiming to find a superior surgical approach were published more than a decade ago.39,40 Both studies showed no differences in survival, length of hospital stay, or need for parenteral nutrition in the ExLap versus PPD groups. The recent Necrotizing Enterocolitis Surgery Trial (NEST) randomized 310 of a possible 992 infants to receive either ExLap or PPD and found no overall difference in the primary outcome of a composite of death or neurodevelopmental impairment at 18 to 22 months.41 Interestingly, using Bayesian analysis, a preoperative diagnosis of either NEC or SIP may modify the impact of treatment, with some benefit attributed to ExLap if a preoperative diagnosis of NEC has been made.
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Management

paragraphs.text: A diagnosis of NEC has a significant negative impact on neonatal survival and other outcomes. Mortality depends on the gestational age, birth weight, extent of bowel involvement, and the need for surgical intervention. The overall mortality due to NEC ranges from 20% to 30%.42,43 The mortality rate of infants who underwent surgery was found to be higher (35%) than that for infants who required only medical treatment (21%). Mortality in medically treated neonates decreases with an increase in birth weight. Such correlation is weaker in infants with NEC who require surgical intervention. The level and volume of neonatal intensive care at the birth hospital are strongly associated with all-cause neonatal morbidity. Increasing volume and level of care were associated with lower mortality, with infants born to lower level units having an increase of 20% odds of mortality.44,45 Further studies are being done on the effect of regionalization of care on outcomes of the premature neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Survivors of NEC have an increase in adverse neurologic outcomes, specifically elevated rates of intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia, and they perform worse on neurodevelopmental assessment. Higher rates of periventricular hemorrhage, intraventricular hemorrhage, and neurodevelopmental impairments were noted in infants with surgical and perforated NEC compared to medical NEC or non-NEC infants.46 Term brain magnetic resonance images
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: (MRIs) revealed that infants with medical NEC had less brain injury than those with surgical NEC.47 Gastrointestinal complications include the development of bowel stricture, short bowel syndrome, and intestinal failure. Seven-year follow-up of the ORACLE Study revealed a 3.6-fold increased risk of bowel problems in infants suspected or proven with NEC. The risk of strictures increases with surgical NEC compared to medically treated infants (65% vs. 37%).48 Intestinal failure and short bowel syndrome complicated 22.7% of surgical NEC.49 However, it is noted that patients with intestinal failure due to NEC have a higher potential for rehabilitation than other causes (volvulus, intestinal atresia, and gastroschisis). Failure to thrive is a common complication and is threeto fourfold more common in infants who develop NEC. Infants with NEC were found to have a significantly higher rate of severe growth failure (<3% weight for age) than controls when the Vermont Oxford Network (VON) database of more than 9000 extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants was studied.50
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: NEC is also a significant contributor to health care costs. The annual economic burden of the disease is estimated to be between 500 million and 1 billion US dollars.43 Longer hospitalization, an increase in the number of required procedures, and other resources contribute to the cost of initial hospitalization. The cost of care for infants with NEC is significantly higher than that of infants of the same gestational age but without this disease.51 Care for infants who have NEC remains more expensive after discharge, as well. According to data from Texas Medicaid, the cost of care for infants with medically treated NEC became similar to that for children who did not have NEC after 1 year of age. Medical expenses in children who have undergone surgical intervention for NEC continue to be higher for 1 to 2 years.52 Outpatient follow-up of infants who have had NEC is vital because of the significant long-term consequences of this disease. Standardized multidisciplinary approaches with particular attention to nutrition and rehabilitation should be utilized.
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: As previously mentioned, we would like to preface this section with the disclaimer that we do not have a good definition of NEC. Therefore the information provided is what is currently available that relates to a form of intestinal injury referred to as NEC that involves a multifactorial pathway, and these may represent more discrete entities.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: NEC pathogenesis has historically been attributed to the multifactorial nature of its development. Several risk factors, such as formula feeding, prematurity, ischemia, dysmotility, dysbiosis, and compromised intestinal host response, have led to one common pathway.43,53,54 What we refer to as NEC represents more than one disease (or endotype). Each of these diseases is being shown to have a different pathophysiology. Considering this, we need to evaluate NEC not as one disease but as various diseases with
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: different pathophysiologies, such as is done in cancer and diabetes. The classic form of NEC is associated with prematurity, with 90% of cases developing prior to 37 weeks’ corrected gestational age, implying that NEC is specific to the developing underdeveloped gut. It occurs at 2 to 6 weeks of age, with the highest incidence of the disease occurring at 28 to 32 weeks of corrected gestational age. Although many factors predispose preterm infants to NEC, prematurity, formula feeding, impaired mucosal defenses, altered immune response and mucosal development, and intestinal dysbiosis are major contributing factors for NEC development.55–57 A concerted effort elucidates the factors associated with prematurity that predispose this already vulnerable population to NEC. Those factors are categorized and described below.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: The ability of premature infants to respond to and control infection is significantly different from full-term newborns. This complicated and interconnected system is comprised of • Physical barriers that prevent intrusion of infectious
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: agents (skin, mucous membranes, epithelium of the intestine with the mucous layer, and biomedical factors) • Innate and adaptive immune systems (including cellular
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: and humoral components) Human and animal studies indicate that the abovementioned barriers are deficient in premature infants compared to term infants and adults.58,59 This deficiency can be quantitative, qualitative, or both for different elements of the host defense. The ability of gastric parietal cells to secrete acid is also diminished in premature infants. Coordination of contractile activity in the developing gut corresponds with gestational age. The mature pattern of peristalsis is not developed until around 36 weeks of gestational age.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: There is a lack of data on gestational development of a tight junctional barrier, but this barrier is thought to be deficient in premature infants.60 The defense mechanisms of the intestinal epithelial layer itself are underdeveloped in preterm infants. This includes decreased numbers of Paneth cells. Paneth cells produce several peptides (lysozyme, defensins, and secretory phospholipase A2) that play essential roles in protecting the intestinal epithelium from bacterial invasion and shaping the microbiome. The ability of goblet cells to secrete mucin is also increasing throughout gestation and achieves maturity at term.61 The mucous layer protects the intestinal epithelium from interacting with pathogenic microorganisms while creating an environment for the growth of commensal microorganisms.62
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: Of particular interest is an excessive proinflammatory phenotype of macrophages observed in patients with NEC compared to healthy term infants. Studies explain this phenomenon by upregulation of Smad7 in macrophages of patients with NEC, which inhibits transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β).63–65 The latter factor downregulates the proinflammatory response of macrophages. Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) can be an essential communication
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: channel between intestinal content and the adaptive immune system. The predominant type of IELs in the intestine of preterm infants is γδ cells.66 They play an essential role in mucosal defense and are significantly decreased in intestinal samples obtained from infants with NEC.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: Another imbalance in the cellular component of the immune system of infants with NEC is a shift in T-cell differentiation with an increase in CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes and a decrease in counter-inflammatory Treg cells.67 Interleukin-17 (IL-17), a product of CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes, leads to increased apoptosis of enterocytes and negatively affects intestinal epithelial tight junctions and the proliferation of enterocytes.54 The CD4+ Th17/Treg disbalance was also shown to result in apoptosis of Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells in the mouse model.68 The B-cell arm of the adaptive immune system serves as antigen-presenting cells and produces immunoglobulins. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is of particular significance, as animal studies have shown that secretory IgA (sIgA) shapes intestinal microbiota and regulates the maturation of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and development of the intestinal barrier function.69–71 Short- and long-term benefits of exposure to maternal sIgA have also been shown. sIgA in human breast milk is considered one of the components contributing to the protective effect of this mode of nutrition, especially in preterm infants. A review of studies that evaluated the potential benefit of immunoglobulins in preterm infants did not show a reduction in NEC incidence.72 It is important to point out that only studies of intravenous immunoglobulins were reviewed.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: Intestinal epithelium, to some extent, can be viewed as a teeter-totter, with the microbiome on one side and the hyperactivated immune system on the other. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) of intestinal microbiota bind and activate a series of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). The roles of human Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and intracellular nucleotide-binding oligomerization domains
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: (NODs) in the pathogenesis of NEC have been under much scrutiny in the last 10 to 15 years.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: TLR-4 receptors and their activation are one of the cornerstones in NEC pathogenesis.56,67 These receptors participate in normal gut development in humans and mice.73 This explains the higher level of expression of these receptors in the developing gut. In premature infants, TLR-4 expression remains elevated after birth and peaks at the same time of highest risk for NEC.57,74 The TLR-4 receptors located on IECs are activated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), abundant in cell walls of gram-negative bacteria that colonize the gut.75 This activation leads to several adverse effects: increased apoptosis, impaired regeneration of IECs, and proinflammatory cytokine response. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress resulted from TLR-4 activation in animal studies.76 All of the above features are essential elements of NEC. Human breast milk significantly reduces TLR-4 signaling in neonatal mice via activation of the EGF receptor, which may explain its protective action against NEC.77 TLR-9, however, seems to counterbalance the proinflammatory response of TLR-4 activation.74 Further studies on TLRs are being done.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: NOD receptors are a family of intracellular receptors present in monocytes, Paneth cells, and IECs.78 Peptidoglycan from the bacterial wall of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria serve as a ligand for NOD receptors. NOD2 receptors mediate the production of defensins by Paneth cells.79 NOD2 activation was shown to inhibit TLR-4 in IECs and decrease apoptosis while improving mucosal intestinal injury repair.80 NOD2 provides a way of communication between intestinal commensal bacteria and the innate immune system. One population-based study from Germany showed that VLBW infants with two or more NOD2 variant alleles were at higher risk of developing surgical NEC.81 Refer to Table 89.2 for the roles of cytokines and chemokines in the pathogenesis of NEC.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and the development of intestinal microvasculature also appear to be involved in the pathogenesis of NEC. One study demonstrated that VEGF level is decreased in intestinal tissue obtained from infants with NEC.82 An animal study also demonstrated the importance of VEGF and its receptor signaling for maintaining the integrity of intestinal microvasculature in the postnatal period.83 Interestingly, the peak incidence of NEC occurs at the same corrected gestational age as retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). This coincidence is intriguing, and whether this relates to the VEGF system requires additional research.
paragraphs.heading: Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

paragraphs.text: Sterility of the fetus in utero had been a well-accepted notion; however, we now know that microorganisms colonize the fetal gut before birth.84 Culture and non–culturebased studies have revealed the presence of microorganisms in the amniotic fluid, placenta, and meconium. Known factors that affect gut colonization in infants are preterm birth, mode of delivery, the use of antibiotics, and breast milk versus formula feeding. The resemblance between fetal and neonatal bacterial colonization on one side and bacterial flora of the maternal oral cavity and placenta on the other side strongly points to the hematogenous transfer of bacteria during gestation.85–87 The microbiome of a developing gut can modify health outcomes of both term and preterm infants for years to come. The intestinal microbial environment plays a crucial role in the development of NEC. Bacterial colonization of the intestine has been revealed as a requirement in developing NEC as bacterial endotoxin identified in the blood of infants with NEC.88,89 The study of gut colonization in preterm infants showed that shifts in predominant bacterial classes are well orchestrated and abrupt: from bacilli to Gammaproteobacteria and then to Clostridia.90 The proportion of anaerobes approached that of older children by 33 to 36 weeks of postconceptual age. Factors such as gestational age at sample collection, mode of delivery, and antibiotic treatment affected only the pace of colonization but not the actual sequence of bacterial classes.91,92
paragraphs.heading: Dysbiosis

paragraphs.text: Studies comparing stool microbiome of preterm infants who developed NEC with matched controls found an increase in Gammaproteobacteria and a decrease in Clostridia and Negativicutes in those infants who developed NEC.6,91–93 A systematic review and meta-analysis of sequencing data from 14 studies showed that preterm infants that developed NEC had increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria and decreased relative abundance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes. Increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria prior to the development of NEC emerged as a critical element of a dysbiotic shift observed in this pathology. This provides an abundance of LPS—a ligand of the TLR-4 receptor. TLR-4 activation, as discussed earlier, is a crucial step in the pathogenesis of
paragraphs.heading: Dysbiosis

paragraphs.text: NEC. Further studies using a metagenomic and multi-omic systems biology approach are needed.
paragraphs.heading: Dysbiosis

paragraphs.text: Most NEC cases occur in infants who have received partial or full enteral nutrition. The disease usually develops days to weeks after initiation of enteral feedings; therefore this form of alimentation was regarded as an important risk factor for the classic form of NEC for decades. Delaying initiation and slow advancement of enteral feedings were used to avoid this dreaded disease; however, several studies have shown that these methods did not prevent or decrease NEC incidence.94,95 Results from animal and adult human studies provide compelling evidence that these practices have a negative impact on the gastrointestinal tract, including mucosal atrophy, bacterial translocation, sepsis, and dysregulation in the secretion of trophic hormones. Neonatal studies suggest that more extended nil per os (NPO) status in preterm infants is associated with an increased risk for NEC and an increase in intestinal inflammation.96,97 In 2022, a Cochrane review dedicated to this question found no evidence that delaying initiation of enteral feeding beyond 4 days of life affects the risk of NEC development.98 This review included 1551 infants from 14 RCTs. Delayed introduction of progressive feeds has also been associated with fewer days on full feeds and increased morbidities such as ROP, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and intestinal inflammation.97,99 When enteral nutrition is initiated, the controversy shifts toward determining the optimal rate of volume advancement. A Cochrane review published in 2021 included 13 RCTs with 4033 infants. Slow advancement was defined as a daily increment of 15 to 20 mL/ kg of enteral feeding volume and faster advancement as a daily increment of 30 to 40 mL/kg. No difference in NEC risk and all-cause mortality was found between the groups. Advancing at a slower rate may slightly increase the risk for infection.100 The recently published Speed of Increasing milk Feeds Trial (SIFT) randomized more than 2800 infants to 18 mL/kg/d versus 30 mL/kg/d feeding advancements.94 There was no significant difference in survival or morbidities between both groups.101
paragraphs.heading: Enteral Feedings

paragraphs.text: Breast milk provided by the mother (mother’s own milk [MoM]) is considered the gold standard of nutrition for an infant of any gestational age. Human milk has been accepted for over 30 years as being associated with a decreased incidence of NEC.102–104 Further, it is dose dependent, with an 83% reduction in NEC if the infant feeds more than 50% of MoM in the first 14 days.105 Meinzen-Derr et al.106 showed that the likelihood of NEC or death after 2 weeks decreased by a factor of 0.83 for each 10% increase in the proportion of human milk in the total intake. Another study showed
paragraphs.heading: Role of Human Milk

paragraphs.text: that the administration of exclusive breast milk for less than 7 days in the first month of life increased the risk of NEC fourfold in VLBW infants.107
paragraphs.heading: Role of Human Milk

paragraphs.text: Breast milk contains multiple bioactive components that collectively confer protective benefits to the growing premature infant. These benefits include augmentation of the infant’s immune system, anti-inflammatory effects, strengthening the mucosal barrier, and enriching beneficial bacterial flora of the gut. Breast milk components include EGF, heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor, platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase (PAF-AH), sIgA, lactoferrin, human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), nitrates, glutamine, and IL-10, among others. Freezing, thawing, and pasteurization of breast milk affect the content of these components and will likely decrease its protective effect.
paragraphs.heading: Role of Human Milk

paragraphs.text: In many cases, however, mothers of preterm infants do not produce sufficient breast milk, especially in the immediate postnatal period, and alternative feeding is required. Human donor breast milk (HDM) emerged as an alternative for the nutrition of preterm infants when MoM is unavailable. A 2019 Cochrane review of 12 trials (1871 infants) concluded that formula-fed infants had a twofold greater risk for NEC development compared with infants who received HDM.108 However, as with most meta-analyses, the outcomes can be misleading because they are only as good as the studies that comprise the review. Currently, there are no adequately powered randomized prospective studies of human milk versus formula that evaluate NEC as an outcome. Furthermore, in a recent review, the protective effect of DHM versus formula to prevent surgical NEC was not demonstrated.109 The Donor Milk for Improved Neurodevelopmental Outcomes (DoMINO) group studied neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants randomized to HDM versus formula and did not find significant benefit at 18 months in a study of 363 infants.110
paragraphs.heading: Role of Human Milk

paragraphs.text: Fortification of human milk products (MoM and HDM) is necessary to meet the nutritional needs of the preterm infant. Studies suggest that feeding only human milk and human milk–based fortifier provides better protection against NEC when compared to feeding bovine products. The occurrence of NEC reportedly decreased from 17% to 5% and surgical NEC from 12% to 1%. However, the studies used in this analysis were not powered to detect NEC occurrence as a primary outcome. In a multicenter RCT, Cristofalo et al.111 showed that infants fed an exclusive human milk diet had decreased incidence of NEC when compared to those fed with preterm formula (3% vs. 21%). However, the control group also received infant formula, which is currently not the standard of care in present neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). Hair et al.112 found that an exclusive human milk diet (MoM and HDM+ human milk–based fortifier) significantly reduced the incidence of NEC, late-onset sepsis, ROP, BPD, and mortality when compared with
paragraphs.heading: Role of Human Milk

paragraphs.text: a bovine-based diet. In one of the largest, nonindustry RCTs, O’Connor et al.,110,113 of the OptiMoM Feeding group, compared premature infants <1250 g randomized to human milk-based fortifier versus bovine milk–based fortifier and found no statistically significant advantage in morbidity, mortality, growth, or 18-month neurodevelopmental outcomes. The most recent Cochrane review comparing human-based fortifier versus bovine-based fortifier revealed that further studies are needed to conclude that human-based fortifier reduces morbidity, mortality, feeding intolerance, and improves growth.114 The use of a human milk–based fortifier does not come without potential disadvantages. Eibensteiner et al.115 reported poor weight gain, longer duration of parenteral nutrition, and delayed achievement of full enteral feeds. In a recent review of six randomized studies, an exclusive human milk diet was associated with lower weight gain compared to bovine milk–derived fortification.116 Human milk–based fortifier requires it to be added at a 1:1 ratio with human milk to reach adequate caloric density, which results in a dilution of MoM. As previously discussed, MoM has a dose-dependent protective effect that may be diminished by the dilution caused by human milk–based fortification.
paragraphs.heading: Role of Human Milk

paragraphs.text: Premature infants are at higher risk of needing packed red blood cell (pRBC) transfusions, with some studies estimating that about 90% of infants with birth weight below 1500 g receive at least one.117 This intervention has long been under scrutiny for its potential role in NEC pathogenesis with a proposed mechanism like that of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), prompting the term transfusionrelated acute gut injury (TRAGI) or transfusion-associated NEC (TANEC).118 Distinguishing whether transfusions predispose preterm infants to NEC or whether NEC is related to a deteriorating pretransfusion status remains difficult. Transfusion guidelines are not uniform, and changes in an infant’s clinical status frequently trigger laboratory evaluations with subsequent pRBC transfusions.
paragraphs.heading: Role of Blood Transfusions

paragraphs.text: Earlier studies found associations between pRBC transfusion and NEC development. This association was reinforced by a systematic review of 12 retrospective studies, although only part of those studies was included in calculating odds ratios. Only five out of the 12 included studies reported unadjusted infants’ exposure to transfusion in the previous 48 hours and NEC, and only four studies reported adjusted estimates of such exposure. Several mechanisms were proposed to explain the role of transfusions in the development of NEC: (1) reperfusion injury due to transfusion; (2) immunologic reactions and injury of intestinal mucosa triggered by cytokines, fragmented RBCs, and free hemoglobin; and (3) transient mesenteric ischemia after blood transfusion. A prospective observational study found a significant elevation of proinflammatory cytokines,
paragraphs.heading: Role of Blood Transfusions

paragraphs.text: including IL-1β, IL-8, interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), IL-17, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10), and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1), at different time points following blood transfusion in preterm infants less than 32 weeks of gestation.
paragraphs.heading: Role of Blood Transfusions

paragraphs.text: Alternatively, evidence has also accumulated about the lack of association between pRBC transfusions and NEC. Moreover, some studies have found that blood transfusions are associated with a lower risk for NEC.119–121 In the secondary analysis of a prospective multicenter study, Patel and colleagues122 revealed that severe anemia (Hb <8 g/dL), but not blood transfusion, was associated with the development of NEC. In one meta-analysis, the authors found that RCT data conflicted with the results of observational studies. The RCTs show that blood transfusions are associated with a lower risk for NEC, and the observational studies show that transfusions are associated with NEC.123 Two large RCTs studying liberal versus restrictive transfusion thresholds (ETTNO and ToP) on VLBW infants did not reveal significant differences in morbidity, including NEC, between both groups.124,125 These results further put into question whether the transfusions themselves are associated with the development of NEC or with the severity of anemia.
paragraphs.heading: Role of Blood Transfusions

paragraphs.text: Administration of enteral feedings during blood transfusion is another daunting issue. A small case-control study found that implementing a policy for withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusion was associated with reducing NEC incidence.126 Another small study looked at trends of mesenteric tissue oxygenation during and after pRBC transfusions relative to feeding status.127 This study found that infants who received enteral alimentation during pRBC transfusions had negative trends in postprandial mesenteric tissue oxygenation for up to 15 hours after the transfusion compared to infants who were not fed. There was no difference in mesenteric oxygenation during the transfusion between the groups. The authors suggested relative postprandial ischemia after transfusion in infants who were fed. It is important to note that most infants who were fed during transfusion were getting formula feedings (six out of eight), and many infants whose feeds were held during transfusion were receiving breast milk feedings (seven out of nine).127 This difference could have had a significant impact on the difference in the NEC incidence. A systematic review recently evaluated the evidence for withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusions.128 This review showed that withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusions significantly reduced the incidence of TANEC (risk ratio [RR] = 0.47; 95% CI, 0.28–0.80; P = .005). No RCTs were included in this review because there were none. Conclusions were drawn by comparing rates of TANEC before and after implementation of the practice to withhold feedings in the peri-transfusion period. The authors stated that the quality of the generated evidence was moderate. A
paragraphs.heading: Role of Blood Transfusions

paragraphs.text: small RCT revealed no difference in splanchnic oxygenation when feeds were withheld, restricted, or continued during transfusion.129 In summary, controlled and adequately powered studies are needed to generate better evidence to determine the association between withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusions and NEC. One might also simply conclude that the lack of evidence to support the existence of TANEC should be adequate not to preclude feedings during transfusions.
paragraphs.heading: Role of Blood Transfusions

paragraphs.text: Developing preventive strategies to reduce the incidence of classic NEC is very important because of the limited ability to diagnose the early stages of the disease and treat it. Below is a discussion of several of the most critical aspects of NEC prevention. Readers should keep in mind that: • Only evidence-based measures should be employed. • Rather than any separate intervention, a combination of
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: measures has the highest potential for decreasing NEC incidence in the NICU setting. Standardized evidence-based feeding protocols have been shown to decrease NEC incidence and improve other vital outcomes such as shortening the time to achieve full enteral feeds and decreasing the incidence of late-onset sepsis and mortality.130–132 The advantages of maternal breast milk and donor breast milk over formula products have been discussed earlier. This evidence should be incorporated into feeding guidelines for VLBW and ELBW infants. The advent of human milk–based fortifier and several studies showing a reduction in the incidence of NEC have prompted centers to adopt human milk–based fortifier to prevent NEC. However, there have been conflicting results from a large RCT and insufficient evidence to support routine recommendation. Human milk–based human fortifiers have also been associated with poor weight gain and a longer duration of parenteral nutrition.115 Currently, a randomized trial is being done to further compare human milk–based fortifiers versus bovine milk fortifiers (NCT03797517).
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: Understanding the role that dysbiosis plays in NEC development leads to developing new strategies to avoid alteration of the developing intestinal microbiome. Antibiotics are among the most used medications in the NICU. Most VLBW and ELBW infants receive broad-spectrum antibiotics in the NICU. These medications alter the intestinal microbiome in neonates.133,134 Prolonged use of broadspectrum antibiotics in culture-negative infants is associated with worse outcomes, including increased risk of NEC, lateonset sepsis, and higher mortality.134,135 One study found an almost threefold increase in NEC risk when infants were exposed to antibiotics for more than 10 days.136 Therefore antibiotic stewardship is a necessary part of the medical culture in the NICU.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: Antireflux medications (H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors) have also been overused in the NICU. These medications are mainly prescribed not to treat the symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux (GER) per se but rather with the hope to decrease the number of apneas and episodes of bradycardia and desaturation in preterm infants. A large study showed that only about 3% of these events follow an episode of GER.137,138 Therefore the prescription of antireflux medications is clinically unsubstantiated in most infants. Additionally, it is shown that prescription of antireflux medications leads to undesired effects, such as alteration of the microbiome, bacterial overgrowth, impaired bactericidal properties of gastric secretions, delayed gastric emptying, and impaired chemotactic response.139 Indeed, an extensive systematic review has shown a strong association between antireflux medications and NEC in preterm infants.140 Therefore routine use of these medications should be avoided in premature infants.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most controversial topic in NEC prevention is the use of probiotics. This seems to be a logical step given the importance of dysbiosis in the pathogenesis of NEC. Probiotics are live bacteria that confer health benefits on the host when administered in adequate amounts. Multiple studies and meta-analyses were performed to study whether probiotics reduce NEC in preterm infants. The latest Cochrane review results showed a statistically significant reduction in NEC incidence and mortality in infants who received enteral probiotics.141 However, the trials included in this review were highly variable in their inclusion criteria, baseline risk of NEC in control groups and, most importantly, timing, dose, formulation of probiotics, and feeding regimen. In addition, few of the trials included extremely premature (<26 weeks’ gestational age) and ELBW (<1000 g) infants. This necessitates caution with regard to interpreting the results.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: The largest randomized, adequately powered, doubleblinded, placebo-controlled trial that showed a statistically significant reduction of NEC in VLBW infants was published in 2013.159 This trial was conducted in 10 centers across Australia and New Zealand. It used a combination of three bacteria in the intervention group: Bifidobacterium infantis, Streptococcus thermophilus, and Bifidobacterium lactis. There were no differences in primary outcomes between the groups (late-onset sepsis and all-cause mortality). NEC incidence was a secondary outcome. NEC incidence was reduced from 4.4% in the control group to 2% in the intervention group (RR = 0.46; 95% CI, 0.23–0.93; P = .03). As seen in previous studies, babies with birth weights of less than 1000 g did not show a benefit. The results of that trial were marred by the fact that, in 2014, the manufacturer recalled the product (Solgar ABC Dophilus) used in the intervention group. The recall was based on a report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that revealed contamination of the product by a fungus, Rhizopus oryzae, which caused a lethal infection in a premature infant. This incident raises a safety concern for using live bacteria
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: in preparations that are not considered pharmaceuticalgrade quality in preterm infants whose immune systems are compromised.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: A large study that evaluated the effect of the probiotic bacterium Bifidobacterium breve BBG-001 on NEC and sepsis was published in 2016.142 This study was randomized, double blinded, and adequately powered to detect differences in the primary outcomes of NEC (Bell stage 2 or 3), late-onset culture-positive sepsis, and death before discharge. There was no statistically significant reduction of NEC in the intervention group. No differences in other primary outcomes were observed between the groups, as well. This study also revealed that about half of the infants in the control group were colonized with the bacterium used for intervention by the end of the trial, raising concern about potential cross-contaminations in the control groups of probiotic studies.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics recently published a clinical report on the use of probiotics in preterm infants that echoes these concerns.143 Most recent trials have not shown a reduction in NEC for those at the highest risk of the disease. Furthermore, a pharmaceutical-grade product has not been established in the United States, further questioning long-term safety concerns. The Canadian Pediatric Society also called for caution in using probiotics in infants with a birth weight of <1000 g, citing the lack of high-quality evidence.144 The European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition noted incomplete evidence regarding the optimal length of treatment and starting time.145 Two National Institutes of Health–funded trials are currently studying pharmaceutical-grade products (NCT01954017 and NCT03978000), but they have yet to publish their results.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: In conclusion, although probiotics remain a promising preventative strategy for NEC, we should not recommend them for routine use in NICUs at this time. Strong evidence supporting specific probiotics that are pharmaceutical grade for NEC prevention is lacking, especially in ELBW infants at the highest risk for developing this devastating disease. The following issues should be addressed: 1. Probiotic formulations must be manufactured under
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: strict pharmaceutical regulations by country-specific agencies to ensure the safety and quality of these agents. 2. Each probiotic strain or a combination of strains must be
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: assessed separately by an adequately powered, randomized, blinded, and placebo-controlled trial before any recommendation for their widespread use can be made.
paragraphs.heading: Preventive Strategies

paragraphs.text: To advance our understanding of therapy and prevention of the entities we refer to as NEC, we must first summarize some of the shared features that differentiate these entities (see Box 89.1). We need to underscore that many of the standard, highly regarded databases available to evaluate NEC are
paragraphs.heading: Some Imposters of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: flawed. These shortcomings must be recognized whenever retrospective evaluations using these datasets are undertaken.
paragraphs.heading: Some Imposters of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: Food protein intolerance enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) has typically been found in infants outside of the neonatal period presenting with bloody stools, flank discoloration, and abdominal distention, which improve after cow milk protein is excluded from their diets.146–148 However, FPIES can also present in the neonatal period. Many of these infants have relapsed after a cow milk protein challenge, and these infants have been diagnosed as having FPIES. This is a non–IgE-mediated disease. Neonates with a disease process like that seen in older children with FPIES were described in a series of preterm neonates, where five atypical cases initially diagnosed as NEC were more consistent with FPIES.149 The authors suggested that FPIES may be underdiagnosed in this population.
paragraphs.heading: Food Protein Intolerance Enterocolitis Syndrome

paragraphs.text: At this juncture, diagnostic biomarkers for FPIES have not yet been developed. Infants and children with FPIES tend to have normal CRP, leukocytosis, lymphocytosis, and thrombocytosis. In contrast, infants with NEC tend to have high CRP levels, low leukocytes, and thrombocytopenia.150 FPIES in infants may also have an eosinophil predominance with hemoccult-positive stools and hypoalbuminemia. Management of FPIES includes removal of the offending antigen by eliminating it from the diet. With NEC, the patient is usually made NPO for several days, requires parenteral nutrition for extended periods, and is given antibiotics. Therefore it is crucial to differentiate the two entities.
paragraphs.heading: Food Protein Intolerance Enterocolitis Syndrome

paragraphs.text: One condition often confused with NEC is ischemic intestinal necrosis due to congenital heart disease. The risk of intestinal necrosis is approximately 10 to 100 times that of the term neonatal population without congenital heart disease.17,109,151 Bubberman and colleagues151 compared preterm infants who developed NEC and those with congenital heart disease with intestinal necrosis. They found differences
paragraphs.heading: Ischemic Intestinal Necrosis

paragraphs.text: in age of onset and peak CRP levels. They also reveal that the anatomic site of the disease differed, as the colon was significantly more often involved in infants with congenital heart disease than in preterm infants without congenital heart disease. Mortality was statistically different (22% vs. 11%; P = .47). Several congenital cardiac diseases have been related to ischemic intestinal necrosis. The most common entities are hypoplastic left heart syndrome, aortic arch obstruction, univentricular heart disease, truncus arteriosus, and aortopulmonary window accounting for ischemic intestinal necrosis.160,161
paragraphs.heading: Ischemic Intestinal Necrosis

paragraphs.text: Intestinal obstruction due to volvulus, intussusception, and meconium ileus due to cystic fibrosis may present with signs and symptoms of NEC, including radiographic features such as pneumatosis intestinalis. Hirschsprung disease may develop inflammatory enterocolitis, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. This can present with rectal bleeding, vomiting, loose stools, and abdominal distention, making it sometimes difficult to differentiate it from classic NEC.152
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Gastrointestinal Anomalies That May Mimic Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: The first studies that articulated that SIP may be a distinct diagnosis from NEC were published more than 40 years ago.71,153,162 One of the main differentiating characteristics is that SIP is often an isolated perforation in the terminal ileum in an antimesenteric position.122 The remaining bowel appears grossly normal. Histologic investigation of SIP reveals an area of hemorrhagic necrosis without the typical coagulation necrosis seen largely in NEC.154
paragraphs.heading: Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

paragraphs.text: The pathophysiology of SIP remains poorly understood; yet, it is clearly a different disease from NEC.155 SIP is typified by an isolated perforation with minimal surrounding necrosis or neutrophil infiltrate. The onset of SIP is usually earlier than that of the more classic form of NEC. SIP appears to be also related to the combined use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, such as indomethacin and ibuprofen, and postnatal corticosteroids.156 However, Berrington and Embleton13 reported that there might be a significant overlap between the two diseases occurring in the first 14 days after birth. There is developing evidence suggesting that the timing of antenatal corticosteroids in relation to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, particularly proximity to delivery, is associated with SIP.157,158 Further studies are needed.
paragraphs.heading: Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

paragraphs.text: NEC shows radiologic features, including pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas, that do not precede SIP. SIP typically presents with a rapid onset of abdominal distention but without predisposing radiological findings except for free air on radiograph. Despite these differences, both NEC and SIP are treated similarly with the placement of a peritoneal drain.41 Because of this, there are many cases
paragraphs.heading: Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

paragraphs.text: where it is unclear whether the bowel experienced significant necrosis as seen with NEC compared to a simple perforation as seen with SIP because no laparotomy was performed. It is therefore unclear which disease process caused the perforation. Contamination of our datasets for NEC and SIP is likely to occur, and often SIP is reported as NEC.
paragraphs.heading: Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

89 Neonatal Necrotizing Enterocolitis

### DIOMEL DE LA CRUZ AND JOSEF NEU

### Introduction

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), first described over 60 years ago, is the most significant contributor to preterm infant gastrointestinal morbidity and mortality. Its pathogenesis remains poorly understood despite considerable research efforts, and prevention and treatment remain significant challenges. Improved survival of large numbers of extremely vulnerable preterm infants likely plays a role, but there are other reasons, as well. NEC is complicated to define. Instead of being a discrete disease entity, it is better described as a diagnostic category encompassing several more discrete forms of intestinal injury and dysfunctions that have yet to be clearly delineated. This chapter discusses historical perspectives, our current understanding of pathophysiology, prevention, treatment, and future directions to differentiate the more discrete patterns of intestinal dysfunction and injury under the broad diagnosis of NEC. Because the authors still do not have a precise term to describe these more discrete injuries and dysfunctions, not all of which involve intestinal necrosis, we will continue to refer to a diagnosis considered to engender an inflammatory cascade in its pathogenesis as classic NEC. The rationale for doing this is based on clinical and laboratory findings that this form of intestinal injury is often accompanied by clinical deterioration and clear signs of intestinal inflammation, including abdominal distension, periumbilical erythema, bloody stools, the elevation of nonspecific inflammatory markers, and distinctive radiologic changes such as pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas.

As discussed, NEC is an antiquated term, and the forms of intestinal injury and dysfunction that are currently diagnosed require a thorough re-examination. These likely cluster under different pathophysiologic schemes. Accordingly, several entities that have been referred to as NEC (“imposters”) will be discussed, along with attempts to explain how they differ from the more classic inflammatory process. In addition to this delineation, we will also discuss some hypotheses related to the pathogenesis of the classic

inflammatory process, means of recognition, possible preventative strategies, treatment, and sequelae.

### Definition of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

Several publications have recently discussed difficulties with defining NEC and the importance of having a more refined definition.1–4 This is highly problematic because a clear definition of any given disease is required to provide a common foundation to study its epidemiology, pathogenesis, outcomes, and effectiveness of treatments. The lack of a clear definition for NEC has complicated efforts to study this disease. The pathophysiologies of conditions currently placed under the term NEC are very different. For example, the cascade of events leading to intestinal necrosis in a term infant with intestinal ischemia caused by a congenital heart lesion is very different when compared to a week-old extremely preterm infant who develops intestinal perforation and a peritoneal drain is placed without seeing the intestine; a 6-week-old preterm infant who develops abdominal distension, bloody stools, and eosinophilia; or a preterm neonate who has recurrent abdominal distension and emesis but never develops pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas on radiograph.

Nevertheless, all of these have been referred to as NEC. Grouping multiple conditions under one diagnostic umbrella of NEC affects the reliability of statistical data collected and stalls efforts to develop effective preventive and treatment strategies. This chapter recognizes the major shortcomings of what has been referred to as NEC but will still attempt to provide an overview of what this diagnosis entails.

### Epidemiology

The incidence of NEC inversely correlates with gestational age at birth, with a higher incidence in babies born at lower gestational ages.5–7 In more than 90% of cases, NEC

develops in infants born at less than 37 weeks. In the United States, among infants whose gestational age ranged from 22 to 28 weeks, the incidence of NEC declined from 13% in 2008 to 9% in 2012.8 In another epidemiologic analysis, data were prospectively collected on very low birth weight (VLBW) infants (≤1500 g or <29 weeks) born from 2006 to 2017 and admitted to 820 US centers.9 Of 473,895 VLBW infants, 36,130 (7.6%) were diagnosed with NEC, of which 21,051 (58.3%) had medical NEC and 15,079 (41.7%) had surgical NEC. Medical NEC decreased from 5.3% to 3.0%. Surgical NEC decreased from 3.4% to 3.1%. Medical NEC mortality decreased from 20.7% to 16.8% (P = .003), and surgical NEC mortality decreased from 36.6% to 31.6%. Primary peritoneal drainage (PPD) versus initial laparotomy rose from 23.2% to 46.8% in the surgical cohort. Other risk factors associated with NEC, such as intrauterine growth restriction, placental abruption, the presence of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and prolonged antibiotic exposure, have been reported.10–12

### Clinical Features

### Presentation

Early clinical signs of what we refer to as classic NEC are usually vague and nonspecific and may include slight changes in vital signs, new-onset or increased apneic episodes, feeding intolerance, and emesis. Deterioration becomes evident on physical examination as the disease progresses. The signs of disease advancement are also nonspecific: hypotonia, respiratory distress, and cardiovascular instability. The abdominal exam reveals distention, tenderness, discoloration of the abdominal wall, and lack of bowel sounds. Laboratory changes are notable for neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and metabolic acidosis. Blood may be noticed in gastric contents or stool. Classic NEC is historically discriminated from spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP) by the age of onset, with SIP occurring earlier in the admission course. Berrington and Embleton13 recently showed considerable overlap between NEC and SIP in those that present early (<14 days), and the two entities may not be accurately differentiated. In a cohort of 785 infants, NEC occurred before 14 days of life in 30% of the infants who had NEC.

### Diagnosis

Diagnosis is made using a combination of clinical, laboratory, and radiologic findings, with radiologic findings being more important for determining the severity of the disease process. NEC was systematically described, and staging criteria were proposed by Bell et al.14 in 1978, with modifications of staging made by Kliegman and Fanaroff15 in 1987. Modified Bell’s criteria are widely used for data collection and research; however, this classification has significant limitations. Stage I consists of a combination of highly nonspecific findings. It significantly distorts the incidence of NEC. Pneumatosis intestinalis, a hallmark of stage II disease, may

be difficult to find on radiographs. Additionally, heterogeneously appearing intestinal stool content may be misinterpreted as pneumatosis intestinalis (Fig. 89.1). A hallmark of stage III is perforated viscus with free intraperitoneal air, which could be due to SIP or NEC. A confirmed diagnosis remains unknown when a primary peritoneal drain is placed and no direct bowel visualization and histologic evaluation are performed. This classification also falls short when NEC progresses without exhibiting pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas. Even with free intraperitoneal air, if only a drain is placed without direct observation by the surgeon, the definitive diagnosis of NEC cannot be made. Several other scoring systems have been developed over the years that may be more useful in diagnosing NEC using machine learning techniques.2 The advent of machine learning analysis has recently led to the development of predictive tools to differentiate NEC with SIPs.16

It is important to note that available modes of diagnostics for NEC can only recognize changes in the late stages of the disease when the intestinal epithelial barrier has already been compromised and the signs of systemic response and deterioration are apparent. Complete blood count (CBC) components held promise as a biomarker for early NEC. Decreasing platelet counts, elevated immature to total neutrophil (I/T) ratio, and elevated or decreased neutrophil counts have been used as laboratory signs of NEC, with none specific to this disease.17,18 Multiple inflammatory and immunologic markers have been studied as potential predictive biomarkers of NEC. Radiologic signs used to diagnose NEC include pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas (Fig. 89.2), free intraperitoneal air, distended and fixed bowel loops, and a gasless abdomen. remain about the sensitivity and specificity of ultrasound in NEC diagnosis compared to the gold standard of intestinal necrosis seen during surgery or autopsy. Furthermore, bowel ultrasound is operator dependent, comes with inter-reader variability, and has the potential lack of 24-hour availability; also, given its relatively innovative nature, many have not received formal training in using it to diagnose NEC. The above factors lead to uncertainty in diagnosing the early stages of intestinal injury, unnecessary exposure of significant numbers of extremely preterm infants to interruptions of enteral feedings and courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a prolonged need for central access. These interventions are associated with an increased incidence of late-onset sepsis, prolonged parenteral nutrition, and hospitalization.

### Treatment

### Medical Management

Because of an incomplete understanding of the etiology of NEC, treatment modalities have focused chiefly on supportive measures such as stopping enteral feedings, decompressing the gastrointestinal tract, using broad-spectrum antibiotics, and correcting metabolic (acidosis) and hematologic (thrombocytopenia, anemia) derangements. Careful attention must be paid to maintaining normal cardiovascular and respiratory functions, which may involve the utilization of mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and fluid resuscitation.

The choice of antibiotics usually depends on practice in each unit but generally consists of two broad-spectrum agents that cover intestinal microorganisms. Anaerobic coverage may be added, as well. A large propensity-matched study evaluated the effect of anaerobic coverage on the antimicrobial regimen.35 Overall, the infants in the anaerobic coverage group developed more strictures (odds ratio [OR] = 1.73; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11–2.72; P = .02). In infants with surgical NEC, death was significantly less common (OR = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.52–0.95; P = .02).35 Antimicrobial therapy may be tailored to a specific microorganism in cases of positive blood culture. The length of the antibiotic course usually ranges from 7 to 10 days. The decision to stop or prolong antimicrobial therapy is usually guided by clinical status and nonspecific laboratory markers of inflammation such as CRP. Few evidence-based data are available, however, to help clinicians determine the appropriate duration of antimicrobial therapy. It is also unclear how beneficial antibiotics are in NEC cases with negative blood cultures. Serial abdominal x-rays monitor the progression of radiologic findings and help determine the need for surgical intervention.

### Outcomes

A diagnosis of NEC has a significant negative impact on neonatal survival and other outcomes. Mortality depends on the gestational age, birth weight, extent of bowel involvement, and the need for surgical intervention. The overall mortality due to NEC ranges from 20% to 30%.42,43 The mortality rate of infants who underwent surgery was found to be higher (35%) than that for infants who required only medical treatment (21%). Mortality in medically treated neonates decreases with an increase in birth weight. Such correlation is weaker in infants with NEC who require surgical intervention. The level and volume of neonatal intensive care at the birth hospital are strongly associated with all-cause neonatal morbidity. Increasing volume and level of care were associated with lower mortality, with infants born to lower level units having an increase of 20% odds of mortality.44,45 Further studies are being done on the effect of regionalization of care on outcomes of the premature neonate.

Survivors of NEC have an increase in adverse neurologic outcomes, specifically elevated rates of intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia, and they perform worse on neurodevelopmental assessment. ### Pathophysiology of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

As previously mentioned, we would like to preface this section with the disclaimer that we do not have a good definition of NEC. Therefore the information provided is what is currently available that relates to a form of intestinal injury referred to as NEC that involves a multifactorial pathway, and these may represent more discrete entities.

NEC pathogenesis has historically been attributed to the multifactorial nature of its development. Several risk factors, such as formula feeding, prematurity, ischemia, dysmotility, dysbiosis, and compromised intestinal host response, have led to one common pathway.43,53,54 What we refer to as NEC represents more than one disease (or endotype). Each of these diseases is being shown to have a different pathophysiology. Considering this, we need to evaluate NEC not as one disease but as various diseases with

different pathophysiologies, such as is done in cancer and diabetes. The classic form of NEC is associated with prematurity, with 90% of cases developing prior to 37 weeks’ corrected gestational age, implying that NEC is specific to the developing underdeveloped gut. It occurs at 2 to 6 weeks of age, with the highest incidence of the disease occurring at 28 to 32 weeks of corrected gestational age. Although many factors predispose preterm infants to NEC, prematurity, formula feeding, impaired mucosal defenses, altered immune response and mucosal development, and intestinal dysbiosis are major contributing factors for NEC development.55–57 A concerted effort elucidates the factors associated with prematurity that predispose this already vulnerable population to NEC. Those factors are categorized and described below.

### Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

The ability of premature infants to respond to and control infection is significantly different from full-term newborns. This complicated and interconnected system is comprised of • Physical barriers that prevent intrusion of infectious

agents (skin, mucous membranes, epithelium of the intestine with the mucous layer, and biomedical factors) • Innate and adaptive immune systems (including cellular

and humoral components) Human and animal studies indicate that the abovementioned barriers are deficient in premature infants compared to term infants and adults.58,59 This deficiency can be quantitative, qualitative, or both for different elements of the host defense. The ability of gastric parietal cells to secrete acid is also diminished in premature infants. Coordination of contractile activity in the developing gut corresponds with gestational age. The mature pattern of peristalsis is not developed until around 36 weeks of gestational age.

There is a lack of data on gestational development of a tight junctional barrier, but this barrier is thought to be deficient in premature infants.60 The defense mechanisms of the intestinal epithelial layer itself are underdeveloped in preterm infants. This includes decreased numbers of Paneth cells. Paneth cells produce several peptides (lysozyme, defensins, and secretory phospholipase A2) that play essential roles in protecting the intestinal epithelium from bacterial invasion and shaping the microbiome. The ability of goblet cells to secrete mucin is also increasing throughout gestation and achieves maturity at term.61 The mucous layer protects the intestinal epithelium from interacting with pathogenic microorganisms while creating an environment for the growth of commensal microorganisms.62

Of particular interest is an excessive proinflammatory phenotype of macrophages observed in patients with NEC compared to healthy term infants. Studies explain this phenomenon by upregulation of Smad7 in macrophages of patients with NEC, which inhibits transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β).63–65 The latter factor downregulates the proinflammatory response of macrophages. Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) can be an essential communication

channel between intestinal content and the adaptive immune system. The predominant type of IELs in the intestine of preterm infants is γδ cells.66 They play an essential role in mucosal defense and are significantly decreased in intestinal samples obtained from infants with NEC.

Another imbalance in the cellular component of the immune system of infants with NEC is a shift in T-cell differentiation with an increase in CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes and a decrease in counter-inflammatory Treg cells.67 Interleukin-17 (IL-17), a product of CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes, leads to increased apoptosis of enterocytes and negatively affects intestinal epithelial tight junctions and the proliferation of enterocytes.54 The CD4+ Th17/Treg disbalance was also shown to result in apoptosis of Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells in the mouse model.68 The B-cell arm of the adaptive immune system serves as antigen-presenting cells and produces immunoglobulins. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is of particular significance, as animal studies have shown that secretory IgA (sIgA) shapes intestinal microbiota and regulates the maturation of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and development of the intestinal barrier function.69–71 Short- and long-term benefits of exposure to maternal sIgA have also been shown. sIgA in human breast milk is considered one of the components contributing to the protective effect of this mode of nutrition, especially in preterm infants. A review of studies that evaluated the potential benefit of immunoglobulins in preterm infants did not show a reduction in NEC incidence.72 It is important to point out that only studies of intravenous immunoglobulins were reviewed.

Intestinal epithelium, to some extent, can be viewed as a teeter-totter, with the microbiome on one side and the hyperactivated immune system on the other. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) of intestinal microbiota bind and activate a series of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs).
