TLR-4 receptors and their activation are one of the cornerstones in NEC pathogenesis.56,67 These receptors participate in normal gut development in humans and mice.73 This explains the higher level of expression of these receptors in the developing gut. In premature infants, TLR-4 expression remains elevated after birth and peaks at the same time of highest risk for NEC.57,74 The TLR-4 receptors located on IECs are activated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), abundant in cell walls of gram-negative bacteria that colonize the gut.75 This activation leads to several adverse effects: increased apoptosis, impaired regeneration of IECs, and proinflammatory cytokine response. ### Dysbiosis

Sterility of the fetus in utero had been a well-accepted notion; however, we now know that microorganisms colonize the fetal gut before birth.84 Culture and non–culturebased studies have revealed the presence of microorganisms in the amniotic fluid, placenta, and meconium. Known factors that affect gut colonization in infants are preterm birth, mode of delivery, the use of antibiotics, and breast milk versus formula feeding. The resemblance between fetal and neonatal bacterial colonization on one side and bacterial flora of the maternal oral cavity and placenta on the other side strongly points to the hematogenous transfer of bacteria during gestation.85–87 The microbiome of a developing gut can modify health outcomes of both term and preterm infants for years to come. The intestinal microbial environment plays a crucial role in the development of NEC. Bacterial colonization of the intestine has been revealed as a requirement in developing NEC as bacterial endotoxin identified in the blood of infants with NEC.88,89 The study of gut colonization in preterm infants showed that shifts in predominant bacterial classes are well orchestrated and abrupt: from bacilli to Gammaproteobacteria and then to Clostridia.90 The proportion of anaerobes approached that of older children by 33 to 36 weeks of postconceptual age. Factors such as gestational age at sample collection, mode of delivery, and antibiotic treatment affected only the pace of colonization but not the actual sequence of bacterial classes.91,92

Studies comparing stool microbiome of preterm infants who developed NEC with matched controls found an increase in Gammaproteobacteria and a decrease in Clostridia and Negativicutes in those infants who developed NEC.6,91–93 A systematic review and meta-analysis of sequencing data from 14 studies showed that preterm infants that developed NEC had increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria and decreased relative abundance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes. Increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria prior to the development of NEC emerged as a critical element of a dysbiotic shift observed in this pathology. This provides an abundance of LPS—a ligand of the TLR-4 receptor. TLR-4 activation, as discussed earlier, is a crucial step in the pathogenesis of

NEC. Further studies using a metagenomic and multi-omic systems biology approach are needed.

### Enteral Feedings

Most NEC cases occur in infants who have received partial or full enteral nutrition. The disease usually develops days to weeks after initiation of enteral feedings; therefore this form of alimentation was regarded as an important risk factor for the classic form of NEC for decades. Delaying initiation and slow advancement of enteral feedings were used to avoid this dreaded disease; however, several studies have shown that these methods did not prevent or decrease NEC incidence.94,95 Results from animal and adult human studies provide compelling evidence that these practices have a negative impact on the gastrointestinal tract, including mucosal atrophy, bacterial translocation, sepsis, and dysregulation in the secretion of trophic hormones. Neonatal studies suggest that more extended nil per os (NPO) status in preterm infants is associated with an increased risk for NEC and an increase in intestinal inflammation.96,97 In 2022, a Cochrane review dedicated to this question found no evidence that delaying initiation of enteral feeding beyond 4 days of life affects the risk of NEC development.98 This review included 1551 infants from 14 RCTs. Delayed introduction of progressive feeds has also been associated with fewer days on full feeds and increased morbidities such as ROP, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and intestinal inflammation.97,99 When enteral nutrition is initiated, the controversy shifts toward determining the optimal rate of volume advancement. A Cochrane review published in 2021 included 13 RCTs with 4033 infants. Slow advancement was defined as a daily increment of 15 to 20 mL/ kg of enteral feeding volume and faster advancement as a daily increment of 30 to 40 mL/kg. No difference in NEC risk and all-cause mortality was found between the groups. Advancing at a slower rate may slightly increase the risk for infection.100 The recently published Speed of Increasing milk Feeds Trial (SIFT) randomized more than 2800 infants to 18 mL/kg/d versus 30 mL/kg/d feeding advancements.94 There was no significant difference in survival or morbidities between both groups.101

### Role of Human Milk

Breast milk provided by the mother (mother’s own milk [MoM]) is considered the gold standard of nutrition for an infant of any gestational age. Human milk has been accepted for over 30 years as being associated with a decreased incidence of NEC.102–104 Further, it is dose dependent, with an 83% reduction in NEC if the infant feeds more than 50% of MoM in the first 14 days.105 Meinzen-Derr et al.106 showed that the likelihood of NEC or death after 2 weeks decreased by a factor of 0.83 for each 10% increase in the proportion of human milk in the total intake. Another study showed

that the administration of exclusive breast milk for less than 7 days in the first month of life increased the risk of NEC fourfold in VLBW infants.107

Breast milk contains multiple bioactive components that collectively confer protective benefits to the growing premature infant. These benefits include augmentation of the infant’s immune system, anti-inflammatory effects, strengthening the mucosal barrier, and enriching beneficial bacterial flora of the gut. Breast milk components include EGF, heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor, platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase (PAF-AH), sIgA, lactoferrin, human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), nitrates, glutamine, and IL-10, among others. Freezing, thawing, and pasteurization of breast milk affect the content of these components and will likely decrease its protective effect.

In many cases, however, mothers of preterm infants do not produce sufficient breast milk, especially in the immediate postnatal period, and alternative feeding is required. Human donor breast milk (HDM) emerged as an alternative for the nutrition of preterm infants when MoM is unavailable. A 2019 Cochrane review of 12 trials (1871 infants) concluded that formula-fed infants had a twofold greater risk for NEC development compared with infants who received HDM.108 However, as with most meta-analyses, the outcomes can be misleading because they are only as good as the studies that comprise the review. Currently, there are no adequately powered randomized prospective studies of human milk versus formula that evaluate NEC as an outcome. Furthermore, in a recent review, the protective effect of DHM versus formula to prevent surgical NEC was not demonstrated.109 The Donor Milk for Improved Neurodevelopmental Outcomes (DoMINO) group studied neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants randomized to HDM versus formula and did not find significant benefit at 18 months in a study of 363 infants.110

Fortification of human milk products (MoM and HDM) is necessary to meet the nutritional needs of the preterm infant. Studies suggest that feeding only human milk and human milk–based fortifier provides better protection against NEC when compared to feeding bovine products. The occurrence of NEC reportedly decreased from 17% to 5% and surgical NEC from 12% to 1%. However, the studies used in this analysis were not powered to detect NEC occurrence as a primary outcome. In a multicenter RCT, Cristofalo et al.111 showed that infants fed an exclusive human milk diet had decreased incidence of NEC when compared to those fed with preterm formula (3% vs. 21%). However, the control group also received infant formula, which is currently not the standard of care in present neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). Hair et al.112 found that an exclusive human milk diet (MoM and HDM+ human milk–based fortifier) significantly reduced the incidence of NEC, late-onset sepsis, ROP, BPD, and mortality when compared with

a bovine-based diet. In one of the largest, nonindustry RCTs, O’Connor et al.,110,113 of the OptiMoM Feeding group, compared premature infants <1250 g randomized to human milk-based fortifier versus bovine milk–based fortifier and found no statistically significant advantage in morbidity, mortality, growth, or 18-month neurodevelopmental outcomes. The most recent Cochrane review comparing human-based fortifier versus bovine-based fortifier revealed that further studies are needed to conclude that human-based fortifier reduces morbidity, mortality, feeding intolerance, and improves growth.114 The use of a human milk–based fortifier does not come without potential disadvantages. Eibensteiner et al.115 reported poor weight gain, longer duration of parenteral nutrition, and delayed achievement of full enteral feeds. In a recent review of six randomized studies, an exclusive human milk diet was associated with lower weight gain compared to bovine milk–derived fortification.116 Human milk–based fortifier requires it to be added at a 1:1 ratio with human milk to reach adequate caloric density, which results in a dilution of MoM. As previously discussed, MoM has a dose-dependent protective effect that may be diminished by the dilution caused by human milk–based fortification.

### Role of Blood Transfusions

Premature infants are at higher risk of needing packed red blood cell (pRBC) transfusions, with some studies estimating that about 90% of infants with birth weight below 1500 g receive at least one.117 This intervention has long been under scrutiny for its potential role in NEC pathogenesis with a proposed mechanism like that of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), prompting the term transfusionrelated acute gut injury (TRAGI) or transfusion-associated NEC (TANEC).118 Distinguishing whether transfusions predispose preterm infants to NEC or whether NEC is related to a deteriorating pretransfusion status remains difficult. Transfusion guidelines are not uniform, and changes in an infant’s clinical status frequently trigger laboratory evaluations with subsequent pRBC transfusions.

Earlier studies found associations between pRBC transfusion and NEC development. This association was reinforced by a systematic review of 12 retrospective studies, although only part of those studies was included in calculating odds ratios. Only five out of the 12 included studies reported unadjusted infants’ exposure to transfusion in the previous 48 hours and NEC, and only four studies reported adjusted estimates of such exposure. Several mechanisms were proposed to explain the role of transfusions in the development of NEC: (1) reperfusion injury due to transfusion; (2) immunologic reactions and injury of intestinal mucosa triggered by cytokines, fragmented RBCs, and free hemoglobin; and (3) transient mesenteric ischemia after blood transfusion. A prospective observational study found a significant elevation of proinflammatory cytokines,

### Preventive Strategies

Developing preventive strategies to reduce the incidence of classic NEC is very important because of the limited ability to diagnose the early stages of the disease and treat it. Below is a discussion of several of the most critical aspects of NEC prevention. Readers should keep in mind that: • Only evidence-based measures should be employed. • Rather than any separate intervention, a combination of

measures has the highest potential for decreasing NEC incidence in the NICU setting. Standardized evidence-based feeding protocols have been shown to decrease NEC incidence and improve other vital outcomes such as shortening the time to achieve full enteral feeds and decreasing the incidence of late-onset sepsis and mortality.130–132 The advantages of maternal breast milk and donor breast milk over formula products have been discussed earlier. This evidence should be incorporated into feeding guidelines for VLBW and ELBW infants. The advent of human milk–based fortifier and several studies showing a reduction in the incidence of NEC have prompted centers to adopt human milk–based fortifier to prevent NEC. However, there have been conflicting results from a large RCT and insufficient evidence to support routine recommendation. Human milk–based human fortifiers have also been associated with poor weight gain and a longer duration of parenteral nutrition.115 Currently, a randomized trial is being done to further compare human milk–based fortifiers versus bovine milk fortifiers (NCT03797517).

Understanding the role that dysbiosis plays in NEC development leads to developing new strategies to avoid alteration of the developing intestinal microbiome. Antibiotics are among the most used medications in the NICU. Most VLBW and ELBW infants receive broad-spectrum antibiotics in the NICU. These medications alter the intestinal microbiome in neonates.133,134 Prolonged use of broadspectrum antibiotics in culture-negative infants is associated with worse outcomes, including increased risk of NEC, lateonset sepsis, and higher mortality.134,135 One study found an almost threefold increase in NEC risk when infants were exposed to antibiotics for more than 10 days.136 Therefore antibiotic stewardship is a necessary part of the medical culture in the NICU.

These medications are mainly prescribed not to treat the symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux (GER) per se but rather with the hope to decrease the number of apneas and episodes of bradycardia and desaturation in preterm infants. A large study showed that only about 3% of these events follow an episode of GER.137,138 Therefore the prescription of antireflux medications is clinically unsubstantiated in most infants. Additionally, it is shown that prescription of antireflux medications leads to undesired effects, such as alteration of the microbiome, bacterial overgrowth, impaired bactericidal properties of gastric secretions, delayed gastric emptying, and impaired chemotactic response.139 Indeed, an extensive systematic review has shown a strong association between antireflux medications and NEC in preterm infants.140 Therefore routine use of these medications should be avoided in premature infants.

Perhaps the most controversial topic in NEC prevention is the use of probiotics. This seems to be a logical step given the importance of dysbiosis in the pathogenesis of NEC. Probiotics are live bacteria that confer health benefits on the host when administered in adequate amounts. Multiple studies and meta-analyses were performed to study whether probiotics reduce NEC in preterm infants. The latest Cochrane review results showed a statistically significant reduction in NEC incidence and mortality in infants who received enteral probiotics.141 However, the trials included in this review were highly variable in their inclusion criteria, baseline risk of NEC in control groups and, most importantly, timing, dose, formulation of probiotics, and feeding regimen. In addition, few of the trials included extremely premature (<26 weeks’ gestational age) and ELBW (<1000 g) infants. This necessitates caution with regard to interpreting the results.

The largest randomized, adequately powered, doubleblinded, placebo-controlled trial that showed a statistically significant reduction of NEC in VLBW infants was published in 2013.159 This trial was conducted in 10 centers across Australia and New Zealand. It used a combination of three bacteria in the intervention group: Bifidobacterium infantis, Streptococcus thermophilus, and Bifidobacterium lactis. There were no differences in primary outcomes between the groups (late-onset sepsis and all-cause mortality). NEC incidence was a secondary outcome. NEC incidence was reduced from 4.4% in the control group to 2% in the intervention group (RR = 0.46; 95% CI, 0.23–0.93; P = .03). As seen in previous studies, babies with birth weights of less than 1000 g did not show a benefit. The results of that trial were marred by the fact that, in 2014, the manufacturer recalled the product (Solgar ABC Dophilus) used in the intervention group. The recall was based on a report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that revealed contamination of the product by a fungus, Rhizopus oryzae, which caused a lethal infection in a premature infant. This incident raises a safety concern for using live bacteria

in preparations that are not considered pharmaceuticalgrade quality in preterm infants whose immune systems are compromised.

A large study that evaluated the effect of the probiotic bacterium Bifidobacterium breve BBG-001 on NEC and sepsis was published in 2016.142 This study was randomized, double blinded, and adequately powered to detect differences in the primary outcomes of NEC (Bell stage 2 or 3), late-onset culture-positive sepsis, and death before discharge. There was no statistically significant reduction of NEC in the intervention group. No differences in other primary outcomes were observed between the groups, as well. This study also revealed that about half of the infants in the control group were colonized with the bacterium used for intervention by the end of the trial, raising concern about potential cross-contaminations in the control groups of probiotic studies.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recently published a clinical report on the use of probiotics in preterm infants that echoes these concerns.143 Most recent trials have not shown a reduction in NEC for those at the highest risk of the disease. Furthermore, a pharmaceutical-grade product has not been established in the United States, further questioning long-term safety concerns. The Canadian Pediatric Society also called for caution in using probiotics in infants with a birth weight of <1000 g, citing the lack of high-quality evidence.144 The European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition noted incomplete evidence regarding the optimal length of treatment and starting time.145 Two National Institutes of Health–funded trials are currently studying pharmaceutical-grade products (NCT01954017 and NCT03978000), but they have yet to publish their results.

In conclusion, although probiotics remain a promising preventative strategy for NEC, we should not recommend them for routine use in NICUs at this time. Strong evidence supporting specific probiotics that are pharmaceutical grade for NEC prevention is lacking, especially in ELBW infants at the highest risk for developing this devastating disease. The following issues should be addressed: 1. Probiotic formulations must be manufactured under

strict pharmaceutical regulations by country-specific agencies to ensure the safety and quality of these agents. 2. Each probiotic strain or a combination of strains must be

assessed separately by an adequately powered, randomized, blinded, and placebo-controlled trial before any recommendation for their widespread use can be made.

### Food Protein Intolerance Enterocolitis Syndrome

Food protein intolerance enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) has typically been found in infants outside of the neonatal period presenting with bloody stools, flank discoloration, and abdominal distention, which improve after cow milk protein is excluded from their diets.146–148 However, FPIES can also present in the neonatal period. Many of these infants have relapsed after a cow milk protein challenge, and these infants have been diagnosed as having FPIES. This is a non–IgE-mediated disease. Neonates with a disease process like that seen in older children with FPIES were described in a series of preterm neonates, where five atypical cases initially diagnosed as NEC were more consistent with FPIES.149 The authors suggested that FPIES may be underdiagnosed in this population.

At this juncture, diagnostic biomarkers for FPIES have not yet been developed. Infants and children with FPIES tend to have normal CRP, leukocytosis, lymphocytosis, and thrombocytosis. In contrast, infants with NEC tend to have high CRP levels, low leukocytes, and thrombocytopenia.150 FPIES in infants may also have an eosinophil predominance with hemoccult-positive stools and hypoalbuminemia. Management of FPIES includes removal of the offending antigen by eliminating it from the diet. With NEC, the patient is usually made NPO for several days, requires parenteral nutrition for extended periods, and is given antibiotics. Therefore it is crucial to differentiate the two entities.

### Ischemic Intestinal Necrosis

One condition often confused with NEC is ischemic intestinal necrosis due to congenital heart disease. The risk of intestinal necrosis is approximately 10 to 100 times that of the term neonatal population without congenital heart disease.17,109,151 Bubberman and colleagues151 compared preterm infants who developed NEC and those with congenital heart disease with intestinal necrosis. They found differences

in age of onset and peak CRP levels. They also reveal that the anatomic site of the disease differed, as the colon was significantly more often involved in infants with congenital heart disease than in preterm infants without congenital heart disease. Mortality was statistically different (22% vs. 11%; P = .47). Several congenital cardiac diseases have been related to ischemic intestinal necrosis. The most common entities are hypoplastic left heart syndrome, aortic arch obstruction, univentricular heart disease, truncus arteriosus, and aortopulmonary window accounting for ischemic intestinal necrosis.160,161

### Congenital Gastrointestinal Anomalies That May Mimic Necrotizing Enterocolitis

Intestinal obstruction due to volvulus, intussusception, and meconium ileus due to cystic fibrosis may present with signs and symptoms of NEC, including radiographic features such as pneumatosis intestinalis. Hirschsprung disease may develop inflammatory enterocolitis, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. This can present with rectal bleeding, vomiting, loose stools, and abdominal distention, making it sometimes difficult to differentiate it from classic NEC.152

### Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

The first studies that articulated that SIP may be a distinct diagnosis from NEC were published more than 40 years ago.71,153,162 One of the main differentiating characteristics is that SIP is often an isolated perforation in the terminal ileum in an antimesenteric position.122 The remaining bowel appears grossly normal. Histologic investigation of SIP reveals an area of hemorrhagic necrosis without the typical coagulation necrosis seen largely in NEC.154

The pathophysiology of SIP remains poorly understood; yet, it is clearly a different disease from NEC.155 SIP is typified by an isolated perforation with minimal surrounding necrosis or neutrophil infiltrate. The onset of SIP is usually earlier than that of the more classic form of NEC. SIP appears to be also related to the combined use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, such as indomethacin and ibuprofen, and postnatal corticosteroids.156 However, Berrington and Embleton13 reported that there might be a significant overlap between the two diseases occurring in the first 14 days after birth. There is developing evidence suggesting that the timing of antenatal corticosteroids in relation to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, particularly proximity to delivery, is associated with SIP.157,158 Further studies are needed.

NEC shows radiologic features, including pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas, that do not precede SIP. SIP typically presents with a rapid onset of abdominal distention but without predisposing radiological findings except for free air on radiograph. Despite these differences, both NEC and SIP are treated similarly with the placement of a peritoneal drain.41 Because of this, there are many cases
